A meteorite crashed through a teenager's Chevrolet Malibu in 1992 after streaking across the US, turning both the space rock and car into collectibles.

September 18, 2026 / 17:06 IST

(Image: Bruno Barral/Wikimedia Commons)

  • Meteorite hit a car in Peekskill, NY in 1992.
  • Event captured on video, aiding scientific study.
  • Car and meteorite became valuable collector's items.

A meteorite that streaked across the skies over the northeastern United States in 1992 became one of the most remarkable documented space-rock falls after a surviving fragment crashed through the trunk of an 18-year-old's parked Chevrolet Malibu in Peekskill, New York. The event was captured on more than a dozen independent videos, allowing scientists to reconstruct the meteorite's journey through Earth's atmosphere and determine its original orbit.

The Peekskill meteorite fell on October 9, 1992, at about 7:50 p.m. local time. Michelle Knapp was at home when she heard a loud crash outside. She later discovered that the impact had damaged her 1980 red Malibu and left a crater in the driveway. A large, dark rock was found beneath the car. NASA records describe the recovered fragment as weighing about 12.4 kilograms, while the Meteoritical Bulletin classified it as an H6 ordinary chondrite.

Peekskill meteorite fall was captured on video

The meteorite was part of a spectacular fireball that appeared over the eastern United States that evening. Thousands of people saw the bright, greenish object crossing the night sky, with several cameras recording it because high school football games were taking place at the time. NASA describes the Peekskill event as the first meteorite fall to be captured on video by casual observers.

The recordings became particularly valuable to researchers because they documented the meteor's movement before the surviving fragment reached the ground. A study published in Nature on February 17, 1994, analysed 14 video recordings of the event. Researchers used the footage to determine the object's atmospheric trajectory, ground path and original orbit.

According to the study, the fireball appeared over West Virginia and travelled about 700 kilometres in a northeasterly direction before the meteorite reached Peekskill. The researchers described the recordings as providing a detailed record of the object's fragmentation and atmospheric effects.

How the Peekskill meteorite turned a car into a collector's item

Knapp's Chevrolet Malibu had been an inexpensive second-hand car before the unusual impact. NASA educational material says the meteorite later sold for about $69,000, while the damaged Malibu was purchased for $10,000 for display. The two objects therefore generated roughly $79,000 combined, turning an ordinary used car into a piece of meteorite history.

The car's unusual value came from its direct connection to the space rock. Unlike an ordinary meteorite found on the ground, the Peekskill specimen had a documented fall, a known impact location and extensive video evidence showing the fireball's journey. The damaged vehicle became physical evidence of that extraordinary sequence.

The recovered rock was classified as an ordinary chondrite, a common type of stony meteorite. Its scientific importance, however, was increased by the circumstances of its fall. Researchers could connect the physical specimen with observations made while the object was still travelling through Earth's atmosphere.

Why the Peekskill meteorite remains scientifically important

The event also provided researchers with an opportunity to study the meteorite's history before it reached Earth. Scientific work on the Peekskill object has included investigations of its cosmic-ray exposure and other characteristics, while the video record has allowed scientists to examine its atmospheric passage and orbit.

NASA has highlighted the fall as an important example of how observations by members of the public can contribute to planetary science. The event was recorded from multiple locations, with NASA noting that the fireball was captured on 16 independent videos. The footage showed the object crossing parts of several states during its roughly 40-second passage through the sky.

The Peekskill fall is unusual because several parts of the event can be linked together: the fireball was observed and recorded, its atmospheric path was reconstructed, a meteorite fragment was recovered and its impact target was identified. In this case, the target happened to be a teenager's parked Chevrolet Malibu.

For astronomers and planetary scientists, that combination makes Peekskill more than a story about a damaged car. It provides a rare, well-documented connection between a space rock's journey through the atmosphere, its orbit before reaching Earth and the exact place where a surviving fragment landed.
